tool.name: PySpark
tool.tagline: Python API for Apache Spark: distributed DataFrames, SQL and streaming
tool.description: PySpark is the Python interface to Apache Spark, the engine for processing large datasets across a cluster with DataFrames, SQL, streaming and machine learning. It is the standard tool for big-data ETL on platforms like Databricks, EMR, Dataproc and Synapse. Learn it to transform terabytes with code that looks like pandas or SQL, and to understand how distributed query engines plan and run work.

glossary.def: The object every PySpark program creates first; you use it to read data, run SQL and change settings.
In PySpark, the SparkSession your program creates to work with Spark, together with its settings such as the time zone.
In Spark, the program you write and start: it turns your code into a plan, cuts the work into tasks and hands them to the executors.
A Spark helper program running on a cluster machine; it runs tasks on its share of the data and can keep cached data.
In Spark, the smallest unit of work: one step of the plan applied to one partition of the data, run by an executor.
In Spark, one chunk of a DataFrame's rows. Each partition is processed by one task, so many partitions can be worked on at the same time.
The Java Virtual Machine: the program that runs Java code. Spark itself runs on it, which is why Spark needs Java installed.
In Spark, a table of rows with named, typed columns, split into partitions across the cluster. It is immutable: changes give a new DataFrame.
A popular Python library for working with tables of data on one computer.
In Spark, an operation like select, filter or join that describes a new DataFrame but runs nothing until an action needs the result.
In Spark, an operation like count, show, collect or write that needs a real result, so Spark runs the plan as a job.
A step of a Spark job: a run of work that needs no regrouping of data. Shuffles separate one stage from the next.
Moving rows between partitions, across the network, so that rows with the same key end up together. Needed for grouping, joins and sorting, and usually the slowest part of a job.
Spark's built-in web page (port 4040 while a program runs) showing jobs, stages, tasks, memory and plans.
A way to use Spark from a lightweight client: your program sends its DataFrame code over the network to a Spark server that runs it.
An uneven spread of data: some keys have far more rows than others, so a few tasks get most of the work and run much longer.
A Spark setting, on by default since Spark 4, that follows the SQL standard strictly: invalid casts, overflows and division by zero raise errors instead of giving null.
A name for a DataFrame that SQL queries can use, valid only for the current Spark session.
In Spark, the registry of permanent table names, their schemas and where their files live.
Spark's default join for two big tables: shuffle both by key, sort each side, then walk through both in order matching keys.
A join where Spark sends a full copy of the small table to every executor, so the big table never has to be shuffled.
A user-defined function: your own Python function wrapped so Spark can apply it to columns. Slower than built-in functions.
A UDF that receives whole pandas columns in batches of thousands of rows instead of one row at a time, which makes it much faster.
Apache Arrow, a fast column-by-column data format both Java and Python understand, used to move data between Spark and Python cheaply.
Where Spark keeps cached data: in memory, on disk, or memory first with disk for the rest.
In Spark, data (or a streaming query's progress) written to reliable storage so work can resume from there instead of being recomputed from the start.
In Spark, the chain of transformations that produced a DataFrame, which Spark replays to rebuild data that was lost.
Spark's query optimizer: it checks your DataFrame or SQL code, rewrites the plan to do less work and picks how to run each step.
Spark's description of what a query must compute, before deciding how to compute it.
Spark's concrete recipe for running a query: which scans, joins and shuffles to use, in what order.
Applying filters as close to the data source as possible, ideally while reading the files, so less data is loaded.
Reading only the columns a query actually uses, which Parquet files make cheap.
Adaptive Query Execution: Spark re-plans the rest of a query while it runs, using the real data sizes it has just seen.
Adding a random number to a very common key so its rows spread over several partitions instead of overloading one task.
In Spark Structured Streaming, the small batch of newly arrived rows processed in one go.
In Spark Structured Streaming, the setting that decides when the next micro-batch runs, e.g. as soon as possible or once a minute.
In Spark Structured Streaming, how late data may arrive, so Spark can finish old time windows and forget their state.
Which rows a streaming query writes each time: only new final rows (append), changed rows (update) or the whole result (complete).
When a Spark task runs out of working memory and temporarily writes data to disk, which makes it much slower.
The library PySpark uses on the driver to call Java objects in the JVM from Python.
The part of Spark that runs physical plans fast, using compact binary rows and generated code.
Spark writing and compiling one Java function for a chain of operators while the job runs, instead of calling each operator separately per row.
A way of storing a table as Parquet files plus a log of changes, adding database features like safe updates and older versions. Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg are the main ones.

concepts.name: SparkSession and the cluster model
concepts.summary: Start a SparkSession, and understand the driver, executors and tasks, and running Spark locally versus on a cluster.
concepts.why: Everything in PySpark goes through a SparkSession, and the split between the driver and the executors explains most of Spark's behaviour.
concepts.body:
A laptop handles a few million rows comfortably. But a company's record of every click or every sale can run to billions of rows: too much for one computer's memory, or its patience. **Apache Spark** splits the data into pieces and has many computers work on the pieces at the same time, in **parallel**. A group of computers working together like this is a **cluster**. **PySpark** is how you drive Spark from Python.

Spark itself runs on the **JVM**, the Java Virtual Machine (the program that runs Java code), so it needs Java 17 or 21 installed; `pip install pyspark` gets the rest. Your Python code mostly gives instructions, and Spark does the heavy work.

A Spark program has two kinds of parts. The **driver** is the program you write and start: it turns your code into a plan, cuts the work into small **tasks** and hands them out. **Executors** are helper programs running on the cluster's machines, each doing tasks on its own share of the data.

Those shares are called **partitions**: the rows are split into chunks, and one task works on one partition. Many partitions means many tasks can run at once.

Every PySpark program starts by creating a **SparkSession**, the object you use for everything else:

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("etl").getOrCreate()
```

`getOrCreate()` returns the existing session if there is one, or creates it. Hosted platforms such as Databricks give you a session called `spark` already, inside a **notebook** (a page where you run code in small pieces and see each result). On your own computer use `.master("local[*]")`: the driver and executors then all run inside one program, using every **CPU core** (each core can work on one task at a time). `local[2]` uses two.

Settings go through `.config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")` when building the session, or `spark.conf.set(...)` later. `spark.version` shows the version. While a program runs, the **Spark UI**, a page you open in your browser at `http://localhost:4040`, shows the work in progress.

With **Spark Connect** (`SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://host:15002")`), no driver runs on your computer: your program sends its Spark code over the network to a Spark server elsewhere. The code you write looks exactly the same.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

print(spark.version.startswith("4."))           # True
print(spark.sparkContext.master)                # local[2]
print(spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism)    # 2  (one task at a time per core)

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "8")
print(spark.conf.get("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions"))   # 8

df = spark.range(1_000_000)        # a DataFrame with one column, id
print(df.count())                  # 1000000  (run as tasks on the executors)
spark.stop()
takeaways: The driver plans and hands out tasks; executors run them, one task per partition
`SparkSession.builder...getOrCreate()` starts every PySpark program
`local[*]` runs everything on your machine; Spark Connect talks to a remote Spark server
pitfalls: Doing heavy work in plain Python loops in the driver and expecting Spark to spread it across the cluster.

quiz.q: Where does the work of df.filter(...).count() actually run?
options: In tasks on the executors, one per partition
In the driver program, row by row
quiz.explain: The driver plans the job; executors run tasks over data partitions in parallel.

concepts.name: Creating DataFrames and schemas
concepts.summary: Build Spark DataFrames from Python data with explicit schemas, and inspect them with printSchema, show and columns.
concepts.why: Knowing a DataFrame's schema and how to define one prevents most type surprises later.
concepts.body:
A Spark **DataFrame** is a table spread across the cluster: its rows are split into partitions held by different executors, and it has a schema of named, typed columns. Like a Python string, it is immutable: every change returns a new DataFrame and leaves the old one alone.

Create one from Python data with `spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema)`. Rows can be tuples, dicts or `Row` objects, or a table from **pandas**, the popular Python library for tables on one computer. The schema can be:

- a DDL string: `"name STRING, age INT, joined DATE"`, the same `name TYPE` pairs as in SQL's `CREATE TABLE` (short and readable)
- a `StructType([StructField("name", StringType(), True), ...])` built in Python code
- left out, so Spark guesses the types from the data (fine for experiments, risky for jobs people rely on)

Inspect it with:

- `df.printSchema()`: a tree of columns, their types and whether each may hold null
- `df.schema`, `df.columns`, `df.dtypes`
- `df.show(n=20, truncate=True)`: prints rows as a table
- `df.take(5)` and `df.collect()`: copy rows into the driver as `Row` objects; `row.name` or `row["name"]` reads a field

In real jobs, data comes from files and tables (next lessons) rather than Python lists. `createDataFrame` sends data from the driver out to the executors, so use it only for small inputs, tests and small lookup tables.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

from datetime import date

df = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("Ana", 34, date(2024, 5, 1)), ("Ben", None, date(2025, 1, 9))],
    schema="name STRING, age INT, joined DATE",
)
df.printSchema()
# root
#  |-- name: string (nullable = true)
#  |-- age: integer (nullable = true)
#  |-- joined: date (nullable = true)
print(df.dtypes)        # [('name', 'string'), ('age', 'int'), ('joined', 'date')]

row = df.first()
print(row.name, row["age"])       # Ana 34
print(df.count(), df.columns)     # 2 ['name', 'age', 'joined']
takeaways: A DataFrame is an immutable, partitioned table with a schema
Define schemas explicitly, e.g. with a DDL string
`collect()` brings rows to the driver; use it only on small results
pitfalls: Calling `collect()` on a large DataFrame: every row is copied into the driver, which has no room for them all and crashes.

quiz.q: Which is a valid DDL schema string for createDataFrame?
quiz.explain: DDL schema strings use 'column TYPE' pairs separated by commas, like SQL CREATE TABLE.

concepts.name: Columns, expressions and filters
concepts.summary: Select, add and filter columns with col, lit, withColumn and the pyspark.sql.functions module.
concepts.why: Column expressions are how you write nearly every change to a DataFrame.
concepts.body:
Almost everything you do to a DataFrame is built from **Column expressions**: descriptions of a calculation on columns, which Spark later runs on every row. Refer to a column with `F.col("price")` or `df.price`, wrap a plain value as a column with `F.lit(5)`, and combine them with operators: `F.col("price") * F.col("qty")`, `>`, `==`, and for conditions `&` (and), `|` (or), `~` (not), with each comparison wrapped in parentheses. Python's own `and`/`or`/`not` don't work on columns. Import functions as `from pyspark.sql import functions as F`; the module has hundreds: `F.upper`, `F.round`, `F.when`, `F.concat_ws`, `F.to_date`, `F.coalesce` and more.

Core methods:

- `df.select("a", F.col("b") * 2)`: choose and compute columns.
- `df.withColumn("total", expr)`: add or replace one column; `withColumns({...})` does several at once.
- `df.withColumnRenamed("old", "new")`, `df.drop("x")`.
- `df.filter(cond)` or its alias `df.where(cond)`: keep matching rows; rows where the condition is null are dropped.
- `df.orderBy(F.desc("total"))`, `df.limit(10)`, `df.distinct()`, `df.dropDuplicates(["email"])`.

Conditional logic uses `F.when(cond, value).when(...).otherwise(default)`, an if/elif/else that is worked out for every row (SQL calls it `CASE WHEN`). `F.expr("price * qty")` and `df.selectExpr("price * qty AS total")` accept SQL snippets directly.

Calling `withColumn` in a long loop (hundreds of columns) makes Spark's internal plan of the work huge and slow to prepare. Build a list of expressions and use one `select` or `withColumns` instead.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

df = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("tea", 3.0, 2), ("cake", 4.5, 1), ("jam", 2.0, 5)],
    "item STRING, price DOUBLE, qty INT",
)
out = (
    df.withColumn("revenue", F.col("price") * F.col("qty"))
      .withColumn("size", F.when(F.col("qty") >= 5, "bulk").otherwise("single"))
      .filter((F.col("revenue") > 4) & (F.col("item") != "cake"))
      .select(F.upper("item").alias("item"), "revenue", "size")
      .orderBy(F.desc("revenue"))
)
print([tuple(r) for r in out.collect()])
# [('JAM', 10.0, 'bulk'), ('TEA', 6.0, 'single')]
print(df.selectExpr("item", "price * qty AS rev").first())
# Row(item='tea', rev=6.0)
takeaways: Build logic from `F.col`, `F.lit`, operators and `pyspark.sql.functions`
`select`, `withColumn(s)`, `filter` and `orderBy` are the core verbs
Use `&`, `|`, `~` with parentheses for conditions
pitfalls: Using Python `and`/`or` between Column conditions, which raises an error.

quiz.q: What does F.when(F.col('x') > 0, 'pos') return for a row where x = -1 (no otherwise)?
quiz.explain: Without otherwise(), rows that match no condition get null, just like SQL CASE WHEN without ELSE.

concepts.name: Transformations, actions and lazy evaluation
concepts.summary: Distinguish lazy transformations from actions that start jobs, and see how Spark builds a plan before running anything.
concepts.why: Lazy evaluation explains when work happens, why errors show up late, and why repeated actions recompute everything.
concepts.body:
Spark operations fall into two groups.

**Transformations** (`select`, `filter`, `withColumn`, `join`, `groupBy().agg`, `orderBy`) are **lazy**. They return a new DataFrame describing a computation, but run nothing. Spark only adds a step to its **plan**: a recipe for the work, not yet carried out.

**Actions** (`count`, `show`, `collect`, `take`, `first`, `write...save`, `toPandas`) need a real result. Spark first improves the plan, then runs it as a **job**. A job is split into **stages**, steps separated by the points where data must be regrouped between machines, and each stage into tasks, one per partition.

Consequences:

- A typo in a column name is caught as soon as you write that line, because Spark checks names right away. But a problem in the data itself, such as text that can't be turned into a number, appears only when an action runs, possibly far from the line that caused it.
- Every action recomputes the plan from the source, unless you **cache** the DataFrame: keep its computed rows stored for reuse (see the caching lesson). Calling `count()` and then `show()` reads the input twice.
- Spark can improve your whole chain at once, for example applying a filter you wrote after a join as early as possible, while the file is being read.

Transformations are also **narrow** or **wide**. In a narrow one (`filter`, `select`), each partition is processed on its own. In a wide one (`groupBy`, `join`, `orderBy`, `distinct`), rows with the same key must be brought together from all partitions, sending data across the network: a **shuffle**. Shuffles end one stage and start the next, and they are where most of the time goes.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

df = spark.range(5_000_000)
heavy = (df.withColumn("sq", F.col("id") * F.col("id"))
           .filter(F.col("id") % 7 == 0)
           .groupBy((F.col("id") % 3).alias("k")).count())
print(type(heavy).__name__)       # DataFrame: only a plan so far, no job has run

rows = heavy.orderBy("k").collect()            # action: the job runs now
print([tuple(r) for r in rows])
# [(0, 238096), (1, 238095), (2, 238095)]
print(heavy.count())                           # 3  (recomputed from scratch)
takeaways: Transformations are lazy and build a plan; actions run jobs
Each action recomputes the plan unless cached
Narrow transformations stay in a stage; wide ones shuffle
pitfalls: Calling `count()` 'just to check' between steps, each time recomputing the whole pipeline.

quiz.q: Which of these starts a Spark job?
quiz.explain: Writing output is an action; the others are lazy transformations.

concepts.name: Reading and writing data sources
concepts.summary: Load CSV, JSON and Parquet files with spark.read, supply schemas, and write results with save modes and partitionBy.
concepts.why: Every Spark job starts by reading and ends by writing, and the options you choose decide correctness and speed.
concepts.body:
`spark.read` is how data gets in: `spark.read.parquet(path)`, `.csv(path, header=True, schema=...)`, `.json(path)`, or the general `spark.read.format("csv").option("sep", ";").load(path)`. A path can be one file, a folder, or a glob pattern like `logs/*.csv`, on your own disk or in online file storage such as Amazon S3 (`s3a://...`), Google Cloud Storage (`gs://`) or Azure (`abfss://`).

For CSV and JSON, **pass a schema**. Letting Spark guess (`inferSchema=True`) reads the data an extra time and can guess wrong. Useful CSV options: `header`, `sep`, `nullValue`, `dateFormat`, and `mode`, which says what to do with broken lines: keep them with nulls (`PERMISSIVE`), drop them (`DROPMALFORMED`) or stop with an error (`FAILFAST`).

**Parquet** is a file format that stores a table column by column, with the column types saved inside and the data **compressed** (squeezed to take less space). Spark can then read only the columns a query needs, and skip chunks that can't match a filter. That makes it the default choice. **Table formats** built on Parquet, such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg, add database-like features on top, like safely updating rows.

Writing uses `df.write`:

- `.mode("overwrite" | "append" | "error" | "ignore")`; the default `error` fails if the path exists.
- `.partitionBy("date")` writes one `date=2026-03-01/` folder per value, so later reads filtering on date skip the other folders.
- `.parquet(path)`, `.csv(path)`, or `.saveAsTable("db.table")` to save it as a named table Spark remembers.

Spark writes one file per partition of the DataFrame, into a folder, plus a `_SUCCESS` marker file. Thousands of tiny files make later reads slow; `coalesce(n)` or `repartition(...)` before writing controls how many you get.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

import glob

with open("people.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write("id;name;joined\n1;Ana;2026-01-05\n2;Ben;NA\nx;Bad;2026-02-01\n")

people = (spark.read
          .schema("id INT, name STRING, joined DATE")
          .options(header=True, sep=";", nullValue="NA", mode="DROPMALFORMED")
          .csv("people.csv"))
print([tuple(r) for r in people.collect()])
# [(1, 'Ana', datetime.date(2026, 1, 5)), (2, 'Ben', None)]

(people.withColumn("year", F.year("joined"))
       .write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("year").parquet("people_pq"))
print(sorted(p.split("/")[-1] for p in glob.glob("people_pq/year=*")))
# ['year=2026', 'year=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__']
print(spark.read.parquet("people_pq").filter("year = 2026").count())   # 1
takeaways: Always give CSV and JSON readers an explicit schema
Prefer Parquet (or Delta/Iceberg) for anything Spark reads again
`partitionBy` creates folders that later reads can skip
pitfalls: Writing with the default mode into an existing path and getting 'path already exists' errors in a rerun.

quiz.q: Why pass a schema to spark.read.csv instead of inferSchema=True?
options: Inference reads the data an extra time and may guess types wrong
Inference is not supported for CSV
quiz.explain: An explicit schema avoids an extra read of the data and guarantees the types you expect.

concepts.name: Grouping and aggregation
concepts.summary: Summarize data with groupBy().agg() and functions like sum, avg, count and countDistinct, and turn values into columns with pivot.
concepts.why: Aggregations power almost every report and dashboard number built with Spark.
concepts.body:
`df.groupBy("country", "year").agg(...)` groups rows and computes one output row per group. Pass aggregate expressions from `pyspark.sql.functions`:

- `F.sum`, `F.avg`, `F.min`, `F.max`, `F.count("*")`, `F.count("col")` (non-null only)
- `F.countDistinct("user")` (exact, but moves more data) or `F.approx_count_distinct("user")` (a fast estimate that needs little memory, using a method called HyperLogLog)
- `F.collect_list`, `F.collect_set`, `F.first`, `F.percentile_approx`
- conditional aggregates like `F.sum(F.when(F.col("type") == "refund", F.col("amount")).otherwise(0))`, or `F.count_if(cond)`

Name results with `.alias()`. Without a groupBy, `df.agg(F.max("x"))` aggregates the whole DataFrame.

`groupBy(...).pivot("month", ["jan", "feb"]).sum("sales")` turns values into columns: one column per month. This is called a **pivot**. Listing the pivot values explicitly avoids an extra job to discover them.

Spark aggregates in two phases: partial aggregation within each partition, a **shuffle** of the partial results by key, then final aggregation. That's why grouping is efficient even on huge data. It's also why one extremely common key can make one task much slower than the rest: an uneven spread called **skew**.

After `groupBy`, output rows are in no particular order; add `orderBy` if you need one.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

sales = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("A", "sale", 10.0, "u1"), ("B", "sale", 5.0, "u2"), ("A", "refund", -3.0, "u1"),
     ("B", "sale", 7.0, "u3"), ("A", "sale", 4.0, "u4")],
    "shop STRING, kind STRING, amount DOUBLE, user STRING",
)
summary = (
    sales.groupBy("shop")
    .agg(F.count("*").alias("n"),
         F.sum("amount").alias("net"),
         F.sum(F.when(F.col("kind") == "refund", F.col("amount")).otherwise(0)).alias("refunds"),
         F.countDistinct("user").alias("users"))
    .orderBy("shop")
)
print([tuple(r) for r in summary.collect()])
# [('A', 3, 11.0, -3.0, 2), ('B', 2, 12.0, 0.0, 2)]

wide = sales.groupBy("shop").pivot("kind", ["sale", "refund"]).sum("amount").orderBy("shop")
print([tuple(r) for r in wide.collect()])   # [('A', 14.0, -3.0), ('B', 12.0, None)]
takeaways: `groupBy(...).agg(...)` with functions from `pyspark.sql.functions`
Aggregation is partial per partition, then shuffled and merged
Give `pivot` its values explicitly to save a job
pitfalls: Assuming groupBy output is sorted by key.

quiz.q: Why is F.approx_count_distinct often preferred over F.countDistinct on huge data?
options: It uses a small HyperLogLog sketch, avoiding the cost of tracking every distinct value
quiz.explain: Approximate distinct counting trades a small error for far less memory and shuffle.

concepts.name: Data types, casting, nulls and ANSI mode
concepts.summary: Cast columns safely, handle nulls with na functions and coalesce, and understand Spark 4's ANSI mode errors.
concepts.why: Spark 4 turned on ANSI SQL mode by default, so bad casts and overflows now fail jobs instead of silently producing null.
concepts.body:
Spark SQL types include `int`, `bigint`, `double`, `decimal(p,s)`, `string`, `boolean`, `date`, `timestamp` (shown in the session's time zone setting), `timestamp_ntz`, `binary`, plus types that hold several values in one cell (`array`, `map`, `struct`, `variant`), covered in a later lesson.

Convert a column to another type (cast it) with `F.col("x").cast("int")` or `.cast(IntegerType())`. Since Spark 4.0, **ANSI mode** (`spark.sql.ansi.enabled`) is **on by default**. It makes Spark follow the official SQL standard strictly (ANSI is the standards body that publishes it):

- Casting an invalid string like `"abc"` to `int` raises an error instead of returning null.
- A number too big for its type (an overflow) and division by zero raise errors.
- Use `F.try_to_number`, `F.expr("try_cast(x AS INT)")`, `F.try_divide` or `F.try_add` when invalid input should become null.

Nulls follow SQL rules: comparisons with null give null, and `filter` drops those rows. Use `isNull()`, `isNotNull()`, or the null-safe equality `eqNullSafe` (`<=>` in SQL). Handling them:

- `F.coalesce("a", "b", F.lit(0))` returns the first non-null value.
- `df.na.fill({"qty": 0, "city": "unknown"})` and `df.na.drop(subset=["id"])`.
- Aggregates skip nulls; `count("col")` counts only non-null values.

To turn text into dates, use `F.to_date("s", "dd/MM/yyyy")` or `F.to_timestamp`, whose patterns use Java's letters: `dd` day, `MM` month, `yyyy` year.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

df = spark.createDataFrame([("1", "10"), ("2", "x"), (None, "5")], "id STRING, qty STRING")

print(spark.conf.get("spark.sql.ansi.enabled"))     # true
try:
    df.select(F.col("qty").cast("int")).collect()
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)            # NumberFormatException (ANSI: bad cast fails)

safe = df.select(
    F.col("id").cast("int").alias("id"),
    F.expr("try_cast(qty AS INT)").alias("qty"),
)
print([tuple(r) for r in safe.collect()])          # [(1, 10), (2, None), (None, 5)]

filled = safe.na.fill({"qty": 0}).withColumn("key", F.coalesce("id", F.lit(-1)))
print([tuple(r) for r in filled.collect()])        # [(1, 10, 1), (2, 0, 2), (None, 5, -1)]
takeaways: Spark 4 runs in ANSI mode: bad casts and overflows raise errors
Use `try_cast`, `try_divide` and friends where invalid input should be null
Handle nulls with `coalesce`, `na.fill`, `na.drop` and `eqNullSafe`
pitfalls: Upgrading Spark 3 code that relied on silent null-producing casts and seeing jobs fail under ANSI mode.

quiz.q: In Spark 4 with default settings, what does casting the string 'abc' to INT do?
quiz.explain: ANSI mode is on by default, so invalid casts fail; use try_cast to get null.

concepts.name: Spark SQL and temporary views
concepts.summary: Register DataFrames as temp views, query them with spark.sql, and mix SQL with DataFrame methods.
concepts.why: Many teams write Spark logic in SQL, and switching freely between SQL and DataFrames gives the clearest code.
concepts.body:
SQL queries and DataFrame methods turn into the **same plans**, so they perform identically. Choose whichever reads better for each step.

- `df.createOrReplaceTempView("orders")` creates a **temp view**: a name for the DataFrame that SQL can use, valid for the current session. `createOrReplaceGlobalTempView` shares it across sessions as `global_temp.orders`.
- `spark.sql("SELECT ... FROM orders")` returns a DataFrame you can keep transforming with DataFrame methods.
- `spark.sql` takes parameters safely: `spark.sql("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > :min", args={"min": 10})`. Prefer that to building SQL with f-strings, which lets crafted input rewrite your query.
- You can also pass DataFrames directly: `spark.sql("SELECT * FROM {t} WHERE x > 1", t=df)`.

Permanent tables are listed in a **catalog**, a list of table names and where their files live (Hive metastore, Unity Catalog or AWS Glue, depending on the platform): `df.write.saveAsTable("sales.orders")`, `spark.table("sales.orders")`, `spark.catalog.listTables()`. Table formats like Delta Lake and Iceberg add all-or-nothing transactions, `MERGE INTO` (update matching rows, insert the rest) and reading older versions of a table.

Spark SQL supports joins, `WITH` steps, window functions, `CASE`, `UNION`, `LATERAL VIEW explode`, plus Spark functions like `date_trunc`, `array_contains` and `from_json`. Spark 4 also adds a `|>` syntax that chains steps in reading order (`FROM t |> WHERE x > 1 |> SELECT y`) and SQL scripting.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

orders = spark.createDataFrame([(1, 10.0), (1, 5.0), (2, 7.0), (3, 9.0)],
                               "uid INT, amount DOUBLE")
users = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "NO"), (2, "SE"), (3, "NO")], "uid INT, country STRING")
orders.createOrReplaceTempView("orders")
users.createOrReplaceTempView("users")

by_country = spark.sql("""
    SELECT u.country, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
    FROM orders o JOIN users u USING (uid)
    WHERE o.amount > :min
    GROUP BY u.country
""", args={"min": 6})

result = by_country.withColumn("share", F.round(F.col("revenue") / 26.0, 2))
print([tuple(r) for r in result.orderBy("country").collect()])
# [('NO', 19.0, 0.73), ('SE', 7.0, 0.27)]
print(spark.sql("SELECT count(*) AS n FROM {t}", t=orders).first().n)   # 4
takeaways: SQL and DataFrame code become the same optimized plans
Temp views name DataFrames for SQL within a session
Use `args=` parameters instead of string formatting
pitfalls: Building SQL with f-strings from values users typed in.

quiz.q: Is spark.sql('SELECT ... GROUP BY ...') slower than the same df.groupBy().agg() code?
options: No, both go through the same optimizer and produce the same plan
quiz.explain: Both APIs build the same logical plan, so execution is identical.

concepts.name: Joins in Spark
concepts.summary: Join DataFrames with the right join type, avoid ambiguous columns, and use broadcast for small tables.
concepts.why: Joins are the most common source of wrong results and slow stages in Spark jobs.
concepts.body:
`left.join(right, on="uid", how="left")` joins on equally named columns; `on=["uid", "day"]` for several keys; or an expression `left.uid == right.user_id` for different names. Join types: `inner` (default), `left`, `right`, `full`, `left_semi` (left rows with a match, left columns only), `left_anti` (left rows with no match), and `cross`.

**Ambiguous columns**: joining with an expression keeps both key columns, and other same-named columns clash. Joining with `on="uid"` (a name or list) keeps one copy of the key. Otherwise alias the inputs, `a = df1.alias("a")`, and refer to `F.col("a.amount")`.

**Null keys** never match in normal equality joins. Use `eqNullSafe` if nulls should join.

**Duplicates multiply**: if a key repeats on both sides, the output has the product of the counts. Check that keys are unique before joining lookup tables (like a table of countries).

**Performance**: joining two big tables normally needs a shuffle of both sides, then each side is sorted by key and the two are matched up: a **sort-merge join**. If one side is small (by default under 10 MB, `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`), Spark **broadcasts** it, sending a full copy to every executor, and skips the shuffle (a **broadcast join**). Force that with `big.join(F.broadcast(small), "key")` when Spark's size estimate is wrong. Broadcasting something large can exhaust driver and executor memory.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

users = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Ana"), (2, "Ben"), (3, "Cy")], "uid INT, name STRING")
orders = spark.createDataFrame([(1, 10), (1, 5), (3, 7), (4, 9)], "uid INT, total INT")

left = users.join(orders, on="uid", how="left").orderBy("uid", "total")
print([tuple(r) for r in left.collect()])
# [(1, 'Ana', 5), (1, 'Ana', 10), (2, 'Ben', None), (3, 'Cy', 7)]

never = users.join(orders, "uid", "left_anti")
print([r.name for r in never.collect()])                # ['Ben']

small = F.broadcast(users)                               # hint: ship to every executor
plan = orders.join(small, "uid")._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
print("BroadcastHashJoin" in plan)                       # True
takeaways: Choose the join type by which rows must survive; semi/anti filter without adding columns
Join on column names to avoid duplicate key columns
Broadcast small tables to avoid shuffling the big one
pitfalls: Joining on keys that repeat on both sides and silently multiplying row counts.

quiz.q: You need customers who never placed an order. Which join type?
quiz.explain: A left anti join keeps left rows with no match on the right.

concepts.name: Window functions
concepts.summary: Compute rankings, running totals, lags and per-group shares with Window.partitionBy().orderBy() and frame specs.
concepts.why: Removing duplicates, grouping events into visits and 'latest record per key' are all window-function problems in Spark.
concepts.body:
A window function computes a value for each row from a group of related rows, without collapsing them. Define the window with `Window` from `pyspark.sql.window`:

```python
w = Window.partitionBy("user").orderBy("ts")
```

then apply a function `.over(w)`:

- Ranking: `F.row_number()`, `F.rank()`, `F.dense_rank()`, `F.percent_rank()`, `F.ntile(4)`
- Offsets: `F.lag("amount", 1)`, `F.lead("amount")`
- Aggregates: `F.sum("amount").over(w)` gives a running total, because an ordered window defaults to a frame from the partition start to the current row
- Without `orderBy`, an aggregate over `Window.partitionBy("user")` covers the whole partition, handy for shares of a total

Frames can be set explicitly: `.rowsBetween(-2, Window.currentRow)` for a 3-row moving window, or `.rangeBetween(...)` for value-based ranges like the last 7 days in seconds.

The classic **latest record per key** pattern: add `F.row_number().over(Window.partitionBy("id").orderBy(F.desc("updated_at")))` and keep rows where it equals 1.

A window without `partitionBy` moves all data into a single partition, which is very slow on big data. Spark warns about this.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

from pyspark.sql.window import Window

df = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("u1", 1, 10), ("u1", 2, 30), ("u1", 3, 20), ("u2", 1, 5), ("u2", 2, 15)],
    "user STRING, ts INT, amount INT",
)
by_time = Window.partitionBy("user").orderBy("ts")
whole = Window.partitionBy("user")

out = df.select(
    "user", "ts", "amount",
    F.sum("amount").over(by_time).alias("running"),
    F.lag("amount").over(by_time).alias("prev"),
    F.round(F.col("amount") / F.sum("amount").over(whole), 2).alias("share"),
)
print([tuple(r) for r in out.orderBy("user", "ts").collect()])
# [('u1', 1, 10, 10, None, 0.17), ('u1', 2, 30, 40, 10, 0.5), ('u1', 3, 20, 60, 30, 0.33),
#  ('u2', 1, 5, 5, None, 0.25), ('u2', 2, 15, 20, 5, 0.75)]

latest = Window.partitionBy("user").orderBy(F.desc("ts"))
last = df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(latest)).filter("rn = 1").drop("rn")
print(sorted(tuple(r) for r in last.collect()))   # [('u1', 3, 20), ('u2', 2, 15)]
takeaways: `Window.partitionBy(...).orderBy(...)` + `func.over(w)`
Ordered windows give running aggregates; unordered ones give group totals
`row_number() == 1` per key = latest-record deduplication
pitfalls: Defining a window without partitionBy on large data, forcing everything into one partition.

quiz.q: F.sum('x').over(Window.partitionBy('k').orderBy('t')) computes:
options: The total of x for each k on every row
A running total of x within each k, ordered by t
The sum of x over the whole DataFrame
An error: sum can't be used over a window
quiz.explain: With orderBy, the default frame runs from the partition start to the current row.

concepts.name: Arrays, structs, maps, JSON and VARIANT
concepts.summary: Work with nested data: explode arrays, access struct fields, parse JSON with from_json, and use Spark 4's VARIANT type.
concepts.why: Event records and data from web services usually arrive as nested JSON, and handling it with Spark's built-in functions is far faster than unpacking it in Python.
concepts.body:
Spark columns can hold nested types:

- **array**, a list of values in one cell: `F.array(...)`, `F.split(s, ",")`, `F.size`, `F.array_contains`, `F.element_at(arr, 1)` (1-based), and higher-order functions (functions that take a lambda) such as `F.transform(arr, lambda x: x * 2)`, `F.filter`, `F.aggregate`.
- **struct**, a group of named fields in one cell, like a small fixed dict: accessed with `F.col("geo.lat")` or `F.col("geo")["lat"]`. `select("geo.*")` expands all fields into columns.
- **map**, key/value pairs whose keys can differ from row to row: `F.col("attrs")["color"]`, `F.map_keys`, `F.map_values`.

`F.explode("tags")` turns each array element into its own row and drops rows with null or empty arrays; `F.explode_outer` keeps them with null. `F.posexplode` adds the position.

For JSON strings, `F.from_json("payload", schema)` parses into structs with a known schema, and `F.to_json` turns it back into a JSON string. `F.get_json_object(col, "$.a.b")` extracts single paths without a full schema.

Spark 4 adds the **VARIANT** type for semi-structured data whose schema varies: `F.parse_json("payload")` stores it in an efficient binary form, and `F.variant_get(v, "$.price", "double")` or `F.try_variant_get` extracts typed values. It is much faster than reparsing JSON strings and more flexible than a fixed struct schema.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

df = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("ana", "py,sql", '{"geo": {"lat": 59.9}, "price": 9.5}'),
     ("ben", "", '{"geo": {"lat": -12.0}}')],
    "user STRING, tags STRING, payload STRING",
)
tags = df.withColumn("tags", F.split("tags", ","))
print([r.n for r in tags.select(F.size(F.array_remove("tags", "")).alias("n")).collect()])
# [2, 0]
print([tuple(r) for r in tags.select("user", F.explode("tags").alias("tag"))
       .filter("tag != ''").collect()])
# [('ana', 'py'), ('ana', 'sql')]

parsed = df.select("user", F.from_json("payload", "geo STRUCT<lat: DOUBLE>, price DOUBLE").alias("p"))
print([tuple(r) for r in parsed.select("user", "p.geo.lat", "p.price").collect()])
# [('ana', 59.9, 9.5), ('ben', -12.0, None)]

v = df.select(F.parse_json("payload").alias("v"))
print([r.lat for r in v.select(F.variant_get("v", "$.geo.lat", "double").alias("lat")).collect()])
# [59.9, -12.0]
takeaways: array, struct and map types with rich built-in functions
`explode` drops empty arrays; `explode_outer` keeps them
Use `from_json` with a schema, or Spark 4's VARIANT for flexible JSON
pitfalls: Parsing JSON with your own Python function instead of `from_json`, `get_json_object` or `parse_json`.

quiz.q: F.split('', ',') on an empty string gives which array?
quiz.explain: Splitting an empty string yields a single empty element, which is why the example removes '' before counting.

concepts.name: Python UDFs and pandas UDFs
concepts.summary: Write Python UDFs when built-ins fall short, understand their cost, and prefer Arrow-based and pandas UDFs.
concepts.why: A careless Python UDF is the classic reason a PySpark job runs ten times slower than it should.
concepts.body:
Spark's built-in functions run inside the JVM, where Spark's optimizer understands them and turns them into fast generated code. A **Python UDF** (user-defined function) is different. It runs in separate Python **worker processes**, extra programs started next to each executor. Every row must be **serialized** (turned into bytes) to travel from the JVM to Python and back, and the optimizer can't see inside your function. So first look for a built-in in `pyspark.sql.functions` or a SQL expression; there almost always is one.

When you do need Python:

- **Row-at-a-time UDF**: `@F.udf(returnType="string")` on a normal function, called once per row. Classic execution pickles every row, which is slow. Execution with **Arrow** (Apache Arrow, a fast shared format for columns of data; `useArrow=True`, or `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled`, on by default in Spark 4.2) moves data in Arrow batches and is much faster, but the function is still called row by row.
- **pandas UDF**: `@F.pandas_udf("double")` on a function that takes and returns `pd.Series`. Data arrives in Arrow batches of thousands of rows, so you can use pandas and NumPy operations that work on a whole column at once. This is usually the best choice.
- **Python UDTFs** (`@udtf`) return multiple rows per input.

Rules: always declare the return type, handle nulls (None or NaN) inside the function, keep functions free of side effects, and import heavy libraries inside the function or at module level, never pickling large objects in the closure. Register a UDF with `spark.udf.register("name", f)` to call it from SQL.
takeaways: Prefer built-in functions; UDFs are hidden from the optimizer and cross the JVM-Python boundary
pandas UDFs work on Arrow batches and are far faster than row UDFs
Declare return types and handle nulls inside UDFs
pitfalls: Writing a Python UDF for something like lowercasing or date parsing that a built-in already does.

quiz.q: Why is a pandas_udf usually much faster than a plain @udf?
options: It receives data in Arrow batches and applies vectorized pandas code instead of per-row Python calls
quiz.explain: Batching via Arrow removes per-row serialization and lets pandas vectorize the work.

concepts.name: Partitions, shuffles and repartition
concepts.summary: Understand how data is partitioned, what causes a shuffle, and when to use repartition, coalesce and shuffle partition settings.
concepts.why: Partition counts and shuffles determine parallelism, memory per task and most of a job's runtime.
concepts.body:
A DataFrame is split into **partitions**, and each partition is processed by one **task**. Partition count sets the maximum parallelism: 4 partitions on a 100-core cluster use only 4 cores.

Where partitions come from:

- Reading files: roughly one partition per 128 MB of input (`spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes`).
- After a **shuffle** (from groupBy, join, distinct, orderBy, window): `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`, default 200, which Spark's adaptive execution (an advanced lesson) then merges into fewer, based on the real data size.

A shuffle writes each task's output to its machine's disk, sorted into one bucket per destination partition, and the next stage's tasks fetch their buckets over the network. That costs disk, network and serialization, so it's the main expense in most jobs.

Controlling partitions:

- `df.repartition(n)` or `repartition(n, "key")`: full shuffle to exactly n partitions, by key if given. Use it to get more parallelism, or to put all rows with the same key into the same partition.
- `df.coalesce(n)`: merges partitions without a shuffle; only reduces the count. Good before writing to avoid many small files. But coalescing to 1 makes the whole preceding stage run as a single task.
- `df.rdd.getNumPartitions()` shows the current count.

A healthy target is tasks of roughly 100 to 200 MB of data and at least two to three times as many partitions as cores.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

df = spark.range(0, 1_000_000, numPartitions=8)
print(df.rdd.getNumPartitions())                    # 8

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")   # show raw settings
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "50")
grouped = df.groupBy((F.col("id") % 10).alias("k")).count()
print(grouped.rdd.getNumPartitions())               # 50  (set by the shuffle)

print(df.coalesce(2).rdd.getNumPartitions())        # 2   (no shuffle)
by_key = df.repartition(4, (F.col("id") % 4).alias("k"))
print(by_key.rdd.getNumPartitions())                # 4   (full shuffle by key)

sizes = by_key.rdd.glom().map(len).collect()
print(sorted(sizes))       # [0, 250000, 250000, 500000]  (hash collisions: 2 keys share one)
takeaways: One task per partition: partition count caps parallelism
Wide operations shuffle; shuffles dominate runtime
`repartition` shuffles to any count; `coalesce` only merges, without a shuffle
pitfalls: `coalesce(1)` before writing a big result, turning the last stage into one slow task.

quiz.q: You want 10 output files instead of 2,000 tiny ones and don't need data redistributed. Which call?
quiz.explain: coalesce merges existing partitions without a full shuffle, which is cheaper when only reducing.

concepts.name: Caching, persistence and checkpoints
concepts.summary: Reuse expensive intermediate DataFrames with cache and persist, choose storage levels, and cut long lineage with checkpoints.
concepts.why: Without caching, every action recomputes from the source; with careless caching, executors run out of memory.
concepts.body:
Because DataFrames are lazy, each action recomputes the full plan from the source. If you use the same expensive intermediate result several times, for example in several aggregations or an iterative loop, cache it:

- `df.cache()` marks it for caching with the default **storage level** (where cached data is kept), `MEMORY_AND_DISK`: memory first, disk for what doesn't fit. It is lazy: the data is stored the first time an action computes it.
- `df.persist(StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY)` or other levels such as `MEMORY_ONLY` choose explicitly.
- `df.unpersist()` frees it. Do this when you're done; cached data takes memory that running tasks also need.
- `spark.catalog.cacheTable("name")` and SQL `CACHE TABLE` work on views and tables.

The Storage tab of the Spark UI shows what is cached and how much memory it uses.

When not to cache: data used only once, data read cheaply from Parquet with good pruning, or huge data that would mostly end up on disk anyway.

**Checkpointing** (`df.checkpoint()` after `spark.sparkContext.setCheckpointDir(...)`) is a **checkpoint**: it writes the data to reliable storage and cuts off the **lineage**, the chain of transformations Spark would replay on failure. Use it in long iterative jobs where plans grow very large. `df.localCheckpoint()` is faster but stored on the executors, so the data is lost if an executor dies.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

from pyspark import StorageLevel

base = spark.range(2_000_000).withColumn("v", F.rand(seed=1) * 100)
expensive = base.filter("v > 50").withColumn("bucket", (F.col("v") / 10).cast("int"))

expensive.cache()                          # lazy: nothing stored yet
print(expensive.is_cached)                 # True
print(expensive.count() > 0)               # True  (computes and fills the cache)
print(expensive.storageLevel)              # Disk Memory Deserialized 1x Replicated

stats = expensive.groupBy("bucket").count().orderBy("bucket").collect()
print(len(stats))                          # 5  (served from the cache)
expensive.unpersist()

spark.sparkContext.setCheckpointDir("ckpt")
short = expensive.checkpoint()             # writes data, cuts the lineage
print("Filter" in short._jdf.queryExecution().logical().toString())   # False
takeaways: `cache()` = lazy `persist(MEMORY_AND_DISK)`; filled by the first action
Cache only data reused several times, and `unpersist()` afterwards
Checkpoints truncate lineage in long iterative jobs
pitfalls: Caching every intermediate DataFrame 'for speed' and starving execution memory.

quiz.q: You call df.cache() and then nothing else. What is cached?
options: Nothing yet: caching happens when an action first computes df
quiz.explain: cache() is lazy; blocks are stored as an action materializes them.

concepts.name: Catalyst and reading explain()
concepts.summary: Follow a query through Catalyst's analyzed, optimized and physical plans, and read explain() output for pushdown, exchanges and join types.
concepts.why: explain() is how you verify that Spark will do what you expect before burning cluster hours.
concepts.body:
Every DataFrame or SQL query goes through **Catalyst**, Spark's optimizer:

1. **Parsed logical plan**: what you wrote.
2. **Analyzed plan**: names and types resolved against the catalog. Unknown columns fail here.
3. **Optimized logical plan**: rule-based rewrites such as **predicate pushdown** (moving filters as close to the data source as possible), **column pruning** (reading only the columns needed), constant folding (computing `1 + 2` once, ahead of time), combining filters and simplifying expressions.
4. **Physical plan**: concrete operators chosen, like scans, `HashAggregate`, `SortMergeJoin` or `BroadcastHashJoin`, and `Exchange` (shuffle), with cost-based choices.

`df.explain()` prints the physical plan; `df.explain("formatted")` gives a numbered, readable version; `"extended"` shows all four; `"cost"` adds statistics.

What to look for:

- **`Exchange`** nodes are shuffles. Count them; each one is a stage boundary.
- **`PushedFilters`** and **`ReadSchema`** on a file scan show filter pushdown and column pruning into Parquet.
- **`PartitionFilters`** show partition pruning: skipping whole `partitionBy` folders that can't match.
- The join operator chosen (broadcast versus sort-merge).
- `*(n)` prefixes or `WholeStageCodegen` mark operators fused into generated code.
- **`AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false`** means Adaptive Query Execution (AQE, next lesson) may still change the plan while the job runs.

Python UDFs show up as `BatchEvalPython` or `ArrowEvalPython`, and filters can't be pushed through them.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

(spark.range(1000).withColumn("country", F.when(F.col("id") % 2 == 0, "NO").otherwise("SE"))
      .withColumn("amount", F.col("id") * 1.5)
      .write.mode("overwrite").parquet("sales_pq"))

q = (spark.read.parquet("sales_pq")
     .filter(F.col("country") == "NO")
     .groupBy("country").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total")))
q.explain("formatted")
# == Physical Plan ==
# AdaptiveSparkPlan (...)
# +- HashAggregate (...)
#    +- Exchange (...)                      <- shuffle
#       +- HashAggregate (...)              <- partial aggregation
#          +- Filter (...)
#             +- Scan parquet  (...)
# ...
# PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(country), EqualTo(country,NO)]
# ReadSchema: struct<country:string,amount:double>   (id is pruned)
print(q.first().total)          # 374250.0
takeaways: Catalyst: parsed, analyzed, optimized logical, then physical plan
Exchange = shuffle; PushedFilters and ReadSchema = pushdown and pruning
Use `explain("formatted")` before running costly jobs
pitfalls: Assuming a filter is pushed into the scan without checking PushedFilters, e.g. when a UDF sits in between.

quiz.q: In a physical plan, what does an Exchange node indicate?
options: A shuffle that redistributes data between partitions
quiz.explain: Exchange is Spark's shuffle operator and marks a stage boundary.

concepts.name: Adaptive execution and join strategies
concepts.summary: Know Spark's join strategies and how Adaptive Query Execution coalesces partitions, switches joins and splits skewed partitions at runtime.
concepts.why: Most slow Spark stages are joins and skew, and AQE plus the right hints fix the majority of them.
concepts.body:
Spark picks a physical join strategy:

- **Broadcast hash join**: the small side is sent to every executor; no shuffle of the big side. Chosen when a side is below `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (10 MB by default) or hinted with `F.broadcast(df)`.
- **Shuffle hash join**: both sides shuffled by key; the smaller side of each partition is loaded into an in-memory lookup table keyed by the join key.
- **Sort-merge join**: both sides shuffled and sorted, then merged. The default for two large tables, because it works at any size.
- **Broadcast nested loop** and **cartesian** (every row paired with every row): used for joins on conditions other than equality, like `a.ts < b.ts`; potentially very slow.

Hints let you choose: `df.hint("broadcast")`, `"merge"`, `"shuffle_hash"`, or SQL `/*+ BROADCAST(t) */`.

**Adaptive Query Execution** (AQE, on by default) re-optimizes at stage boundaries using real runtime statistics:

- **Coalescing shuffle partitions**: merges many tiny post-shuffle partitions into ones of a sensible size (`advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`, 64 MB by default), so the 200-partition default rarely matters.
- **Switching join strategy**: converts a sort-merge join into a broadcast join when a side turns out to be small after filtering.
- **Skew join handling**: splits partitions much larger than the median into smaller tasks.

For skew AQE can't fix, such as a giant null or default key, filter it out, handle it separately, or **salt** the key: add a random suffix to the key on the big side, and copy each small-side row once per suffix.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

def plan(df):
    return df._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()

facts = spark.range(200_000).withColumn("k", F.col("id") % 1000)
dims = spark.range(1000).withColumnRenamed("id", "k").withColumn("name", F.concat(F.lit("n"), "k"))

auto = facts.join(dims, "k")                   # dims is small: broadcast chosen
print("BroadcastHashJoin" in plan(auto))       # True

merged = facts.join(dims.hint("merge"), "k")   # force a sort-merge join
print(len(merged.collect()))                   # 200000  (run it so AQE can re-plan)
p = plan(merged)
print("SortMergeJoin" in p, "isFinalPlan=true" in p)   # True True
print("AQEShuffleRead coalesced" in p)
# True: AQE merged the 200 tiny shuffle partitions after seeing real sizes
takeaways: Broadcast hash, shuffle hash and sort-merge joins each fit different sizes
AQE coalesces partitions, switches joins and splits skew at runtime
Salt or isolate extreme hot keys AQE can't fix
pitfalls: Forcing a broadcast of a table that is large in memory and crashing executors or the driver.

quiz.q: Which AQE feature makes the default of 200 shuffle partitions mostly harmless for small data?
quiz.explain: AQE merges small shuffle partitions based on actual sizes after the shuffle.

concepts.name: Arrow, toPandas and pandas function APIs
concepts.summary: Move data between Spark and pandas efficiently with Arrow, and run pandas code per group or partition with applyInPandas and mapInPandas.
concepts.why: Data scientists constantly cross between Spark and pandas; doing it with Arrow and the function APIs keeps it fast and scalable.
concepts.body:
**Arrow** is the bridge between the JVM and Python. With `spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled` turned on (the default in Spark 4.2; older versions and some platforms need it set explicitly), `df.toPandas()` and `spark.createDataFrame(pandas_df)` transfer columnar batches instead of pickled rows, often 10 to 100 times faster. `toPandas()` still collects everything to the driver, so use it only on results that fit in driver memory.

For pandas logic that should run **on the executors**, use the pandas function APIs:

- `df.groupBy("store").applyInPandas(func, schema)`: `func` receives one group as a pandas DataFrame and returns a DataFrame. Use it for per-group models, custom resampling or anything groupwise that built-ins can't do. Each group must fit in an executor's memory.
- `df.mapInPandas(func, schema)`: `func` receives an iterator of pandas DataFrames (Arrow batches) for each partition and yields DataFrames. Great for running a trained machine-learning model over many rows, loading the model once per partition.
- `df.groupBy(...).cogroup(other.groupBy(...)).applyInPandas(...)` for two DataFrames.
- Arrow-native variants such as `mapInArrow` pass PyArrow RecordBatches.

The **pandas API on Spark** (`import pyspark.pandas as ps`) offers pandas syntax on distributed data, for example `ps.read_parquet(...)` and `psdf.groupby(...).mean()`, convenient for porting pandas code, though native Spark DataFrames give more control.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

import pandas as pd

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")
df = spark.createDataFrame(pd.DataFrame({
    "store": ["A", "A", "A", "B", "B"],
    "day": [1, 2, 3, 1, 2],
    "sales": [10.0, 12.0, 20.0, 5.0, 7.0],
}))

def zscore(g: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:        # runs on executors, per store
    return g.assign(z=((g.sales - g.sales.mean()) / g.sales.std()).round(2))
scored = df.groupBy("store").applyInPandas(
    zscore, schema="store string, day long, sales double, z double")
print(scored.orderBy("store", "day").toPandas()["z"].tolist())
# [-0.76, -0.38, 1.13, -0.71, 0.71]

def add_tax(batches):                                # one iterator per partition
    for pdf in batches:
        yield pdf.assign(gross=pdf.sales * 1.25)
print(df.mapInPandas(add_tax, "store string, day long, sales double, gross double")
        .agg(F.sum("gross")).first()[0])             # 67.5
takeaways: Enable Arrow for fast `toPandas` and `createDataFrame(pandas_df)`
`applyInPandas` runs pandas per group; `mapInPandas` per partition batch
`toPandas` collects to the driver: only for results that fit
pitfalls: Calling `toPandas()` on a huge DataFrame to run pandas code, instead of `applyInPandas` on executors.

quiz.q: You need to fit a small model per store on 2 TB of data. Best approach?
options: collect() and fit on the driver
quiz.explain: applyInPandas runs the per-group pandas function in parallel on executors.

concepts.name: Structured Streaming
concepts.summary: Handle data that keeps arriving with readStream and writeStream: triggers, output modes, checkpoints and watermarks for late data.
concepts.why: Continuously updated data pipelines and live dashboards, fed by message systems like Kafka or by new files, use the same DataFrame code you already know.
concepts.body:
Some data never stops arriving: clicks, payments, sensor readings. That is a **stream**. **Structured Streaming** treats a stream as a table that keeps growing at the bottom. You write a normal DataFrame query, and Spark runs it incrementally as new data arrives.

- Sources: `spark.readStream.format("kafka" | "parquet" | "json" | "rate" ...)`. File sources need a schema.
- Sinks: `df.writeStream.format("parquet" | "kafka" | "delta" | "console" | "memory")`, or `foreachBatch(func)` to run any normal DataFrame code on each **micro-batch** (the small batch of new rows Spark handles in one go), such as a MERGE into a table.
- **Output mode**: `append` (only new final rows), `update` (changed rows), `complete` (the whole result, for small aggregations).
- **Trigger**, when the next micro-batch runs: by default as soon as the previous one finishes, `processingTime="1 minute"`, or `availableNow=True` to process everything available and stop, which is great for scheduled incremental jobs.
- **Checkpoint location** (`option("checkpointLocation", path)`): stores how far it has read in each source, plus any running totals, so a restarted query continues exactly where it left off. Each query needs its own.

Aggregations over event time (when each event happened) keep **state**: running results held between micro-batches. A **watermark**, `withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")`, tells Spark how late data may arrive, so it can finalize old windows, emit them in append mode and drop their state. Without one, state grows forever.

`query.status`, `query.lastProgress` and the Structured Streaming tab in the UI monitor a running query; `query.stop()` ends it.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

import json, os, shutil

shutil.rmtree("in", ignore_errors=True); os.makedirs("in")
for i, ts in enumerate(["2026-01-01 10:01:00", "2026-01-01 10:04:00", "2026-01-01 10:12:00"]):
    with open(f"in/e{i}.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump({"ts": ts, "user": f"u{i % 2}", "amount": 10 * (i + 1)}, f)

events = (spark.readStream.schema("ts TIMESTAMP, user STRING, amount INT").json("in")
          .withWatermark("ts", "5 minutes"))
per_window = events.groupBy(F.window("ts", "10 minutes")).agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))

query = (per_window.writeStream.outputMode("update").format("memory")
         .queryName("totals").option("checkpointLocation", "ckpt_stream")
         .trigger(availableNow=True).start())
query.awaitTermination()

rows = spark.sql("SELECT window.start AS start, total FROM totals ORDER BY start").collect()
print([(r.start.strftime("%H:%M"), r.total) for r in rows])
# [('10:00', 30), ('10:10', 30)]
takeaways: Streams are unbounded tables processed incrementally
Checkpoints make restarts exactly-once; one location per query
Watermarks bound state and let windows be finalized
pitfalls: Running a streaming aggregation without a watermark, so the state Spark keeps grows until the job fails.

quiz.q: What does trigger(availableNow=True) do?
options: Runs a micro-batch every second forever
Processes all data available now (possibly in several batches), then stops
quiz.explain: availableNow is for scheduled incremental runs: catch up on everything, then terminate.

concepts.name: Spark UI, memory model and tuning
concepts.summary: Diagnose jobs in the Spark UI (stages, tasks, skew, spill) and tune executor memory, cores and key SQL settings.
concepts.why: Expert Spark work is mostly diagnosis: finding the slow stage, the skewed task or the spilling shuffle, and fixing the right setting.
concepts.body:
The **Spark UI** (port 4040 for a running app, or the History Server afterwards) is the main diagnostic tool:

- **Jobs and Stages**: find the stage that takes the time. Stage boundaries are shuffles.
- **Task summary**: compare max with median task duration and input size. A max many times the median means **skew**.
- **Spill (memory/disk)**: tasks ran out of working memory and had to write data to disk temporarily, called a **spill**; partitions are too large.
- **Shuffle read/write sizes**: how much data crosses the network.
- **SQL tab**: the executed plan with row counts and timings per operator, including AQE changes.
- **Executors**: garbage collection time (Java freeing unused memory), memory, failed tasks.

**Executor memory model**: `spark.executor.memory` sets the JVM heap, the memory Java objects live in. About 300 MB is reserved; then `spark.memory.fraction` (0.6) of the rest forms one **unified region** shared by execution (shuffles, joins, sorts, aggregations) and storage (cached data). Execution can push cached data out when it needs room. The remainder holds Spark's and your own objects.

Memory outside the heap, for non-Java code and the Python programs that run UDFs, comes from `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` (or `spark.executor.pyspark.memory`). If it is too small, the cluster kills the executor for using more memory than it asked for.

Tuning priorities: fix the data first (pruning, filter early, avoid skew, right file sizes), then partitioning (`advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`, `maxPartitionBytes`), then join strategy, and only then resources: typically 4 to 5 cores per executor, with memory per core sized to partition size.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

skewed = spark.range(400_000).withColumn(
    "k", F.when(F.col("id") < 300_000, 0).otherwise(F.col("id") % 100))

per_part = (skewed.repartition(8, "k")
            .withColumn("pid", F.spark_partition_id())
            .groupBy("pid").count().orderBy(F.desc("count")).collect())
sizes = [r["count"] for r in per_part]
print(sizes[0], sorted(sizes)[len(sizes) // 2])      # one huge partition vs a small median
print(sizes[0] > 10 * sorted(sizes)[len(sizes) // 2])   # True -> skew

salted = (skewed.withColumn("salt", (F.rand(seed=7) * 8).cast("int"))
          .repartition(8, "k", "salt")
          .groupBy(F.spark_partition_id().alias("pid")).count().collect())
print(max(r["count"] for r in salted) < sizes[0])     # True: work spread out

print(spark.conf.get("spark.memory.fraction", "0.6"))   # 0.6
takeaways: Find the slow stage, then compare max vs median tasks to spot skew
Spill means partitions too large for execution memory
Unified memory: execution and storage share `spark.memory.fraction` of the heap
pitfalls: Raising executor memory to hide skew or oversized partitions instead of fixing the data layout.

quiz.q: In a stage's task summary, median duration is 2 s and max is 9 minutes with 50x the input. Most likely cause?
options: Data skew on the shuffle key
quiz.explain: One task processing far more data than the rest is the signature of skew.

concepts.name: How PySpark talks to the JVM
concepts.summary: Understand Py4J on the driver, Python worker processes on executors, serialization paths, and how Spark Connect changes the architecture.
concepts.why: Knowing where Python actually runs explains PySpark's performance cliffs, memory errors and confusing error messages.
concepts.body:
Spark itself runs on the JVM. PySpark is a thin layer around it.

**On the driver**, your Python process talks to a JVM through **Py4J**, a bridge that passes calls over a local network connection. A DataFrame in Python is a wrapper around a JVM object (visible as `df._jdf`). Calls like `df.filter(...)` just forward to the JVM, which builds and optimizes the plan. Pure DataFrame code therefore runs at JVM speed regardless of Python.

**On executors**, Python runs only when needed: for Python UDFs, pandas UDFs, `applyInPandas`, `mapInPandas` and RDD operations with lambdas. The executor JVM launches Python worker processes (reused across tasks when `spark.python.worker.reuse` is on) and sends rows to them, pickled for classic UDFs or as Arrow batches for pandas UDFs. That data crossing is the cost of Python UDFs, and Python worker memory sits outside the JVM heap, so it must fit in the executor's extra (overhead) memory setting.

Consequences: functions sent to executors are pickled with cloudpickle, so closures must be serializable and should not capture big objects (use broadcast variables or load once per partition). Python exceptions on executors come back wrapped in long JVM stack traces; look for the `PythonException` part.

**Spark Connect** replaces Py4J with gRPC, a standard way for programs to call each other over the network. The Python client builds unresolved plans as protobuf messages (a compact binary format) and sends them to a remote Spark server. The client is lightweight (`pyspark-client`), can't touch `_jdf` or the SparkContext, and survives server-side upgrades.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

import os

df = spark.range(3)
print(type(df._jdf).__name__)                      # JavaObject  (a Py4J proxy)
print(df._jdf.getClass().getSimpleName())          # Dataset     (the JVM DataFrame)

driver_pid = os.getpid()

@F.udf("int")
def worker_pid(_):
    import os
    return os.getpid()          # runs inside a Python worker on the executor

pids = {r[0] for r in df.select(worker_pid("id")).collect()}
print(driver_pid not in pids)                      # True: UDFs run in separate processes

plan = df.select(worker_pid("id"))._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
print("EvalPython" in plan)    # True  (BatchEvalPython or ArrowEvalPython: rows go to Python)
takeaways: Driver: Python wraps JVM objects through Py4J; DataFrame code runs in the JVM
Executors start Python workers only for UDFs and pandas APIs
Spark Connect replaces Py4J with a gRPC client-server protocol
pitfalls: Capturing a large Python object in a UDF closure, so it is pickled and shipped with every task.

quiz.q: A job uses only DataFrame transformations and built-in functions. Where does Python code run on the executors?
options: Nowhere: the plan executes entirely in the JVM
quiz.explain: Without UDFs or pandas APIs, executors never start Python workers for the query.

concepts.name: Tungsten, codegen and columnar execution
concepts.summary: See how Spark executes plans: Tungsten's binary row format, whole-stage code generation, vectorized Parquet reads and off-heap memory.
concepts.why: These engine features explain why built-in expressions beat UDFs by large factors and how to read low-level plan details.
concepts.body:
Once Catalyst has a physical plan, **Tungsten**, the part of Spark that actually runs it, makes it fast.

**UnsafeRow binary format**: rows are stored as compact byte arrays managed by Spark, not as JVM objects. That reduces garbage collection pressure and memory use, and lets sorts and hash aggregations work directly on bytes. Memory can be on-heap or off-heap (`spark.memory.offHeap.enabled`).

**Whole-stage code generation**: instead of calling each operator separately for every row (the classic "Volcano" model), Spark fuses a chain of operators, such as scan, filter, project and partial aggregate, into one generated Java function with tight loops, compiled while the job runs by Janino, a small built-in Java compiler. In `explain()` output, operators prefixed with `*(n)` belong to codegen stage n. `df.explain("codegen")` prints the generated code. Python UDFs, some complex expressions and very wide plans break codegen into pieces.

**Vectorized columnar reading**: Parquet and ORC are decoded in batches into column vectors rather than row by row (`spark.sql.parquet.enableVectorizedReader`).

**Other runtime techniques**: dynamic partition pruning uses join results to skip partitions of the other table, and runtime bloom filters reduce shuffle data.

Vendor engines such as Databricks Photon, and open-source native accelerators like Apache Gluten and DataFusion Comet, replace this JVM execution with native vectorized code while keeping the same Spark plans.
concepts.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")   # show the static plan
q = (spark.range(10_000_000)
     .filter(F.col("id") % 3 == 0)
     .select((F.col("id") * 2).alias("x"))
     .agg(F.sum("x")))
print(q.first()[0])                     # 33333336666666

plan = q._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
print("*(1) Filter" in plan)            # True: operators fused into codegen stage 1

q.explain("codegen")
# Found 2 WholeStageCodegen subtrees.
# == Subtree 1 / 2 (maxMethodCodeSize:...) ==
# *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[partial_sum(x#4L)], ...)
# +- *(1) Project [(id#0L * 2) AS x#4L]
#    +- *(1) Filter ((id#0L % 3) = 0)
#       +- *(1) Range (0, 10000000, step=1, splits=2)
# Generated code:
# /* 001 */ public Object generate(Object[] references) { ...
takeaways: Tungsten stores rows as compact binary UnsafeRows to cut GC
Whole-stage codegen fuses operators into one generated function (`*(n)` in plans)
Parquet/ORC are read in vectorized column batches
pitfalls: Inserting Python UDFs into hot paths, which breaks code generation and adds serialization.

quiz.q: What does a '*(2)' prefix on operators in a physical plan mean?
options: The operators are part of whole-stage codegen stage 2, fused into one generated function
quiz.explain: The star and number mark operators compiled together by whole-stage code generation.
